title: How lasers could help provide fuel for nuclear reactors
gist: A geopolitical shift away from Russian-dominated uranium enrichment, combined with maturing laser technology, is opening the door for US startups like Global Laser Enrichment and LIS Technologies to build laser-based uranium enrichment capacity as an alternative to centrifuges.

insights.claim: Laser enrichment separates uranium isotopes by exploiting the fact that different isotopes (like U-235 vs U-238) vibrate and rotate at distinct atomic-scale frequencies, allowing a laser to selectively excite the target isotope's molecules so they can then be separated using chemical or physical methods.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: This is a fundamentally different separation mechanism than centrifuges, which could lower capital intensity and open enrichment to new entrants beyond the traditional centrifuge incumbents.
insights.locator: Laser enrichment, on the other hand, takes advantage of the fact that all molecules vibrate

insights.claim: A full-scale laser enrichment plant from Global Laser Enrichment (GLE) would need fewer than a thousand processing units, versus the many thousands of centrifuges required by an equivalent conventional centrifugation plant, which should lower both up-front investment and operating costs, partly because the laser process uses less energy.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Lower capex/opex per unit of enrichment capacity could make laser enrichment startups cost-competitive with, or cheaper than, entrenched centrifuge operators over time.
insights.locator: While each one of its units is more complex and expensive than a centrifuge

insights.claim: GLE has declined to disclose the specific mechanics of its laser enrichment process, which are classified, limiting outside verification of its technical claims.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Investors should treat GLE's efficiency and cost claims with some caution until independent, commercial-scale validation is available.
insights.locator: The details of GLE’s specific technology are classified

insights.claim: Laser enrichment has been of research interest for decades, but early lasers were high-maintenance, unstable, and difficult to operate; dramatic improvements in laser technology have now made laser enrichment a commercially attractive prospect that it was not during earlier research phases.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: The technology-readiness barrier that previously blocked laser enrichment has eased, making now a more plausible entry window for new commercial ventures.
insights.locator: However, in their early days lasers tended to be high-maintenance

themes.theme: Geopolitical Shift Away From Russian Enrichment

insights.claim: Russia has historically held the largest uranium enrichment capacity in the world and has dominated the market, and its willingness to flood the world with enriched uranium discouraged Western companies from building new enrichment plants.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Russian oversupply was the structural reason the West underinvested in enrichment capacity for years; that dynamic is now the central risk factor for global fuel supply.
insights.quote: Nobody in the West was going to build a new enrichment plant while the Russians flooded the world with enriched uranium.
insights.locator: There’s been interest in using lasers for uranium enrichment for decades

insights.claim: Since the start of the Ukraine war, the US and UK have taken steps to limit or ban imports of Russian uranium, which has opened the door for companies to build new enrichment operations in the West, including ones using new technologies like laser enrichment.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Sanctions-driven decoupling from Russian enrichment supply is a durable policy tailwind for Western enrichment startups, independent of the technology's ultimate cost advantage.
insights.locator: Since the start of the Ukraine war, however, countries including the US and UK

insights.claim: Demand for enriched uranium fuel is rising as countries look beyond Russia for supply, and the widening gap between demand and available non-Russian supply is exactly the opportunity new enrichment technologies like laser enrichment are positioned to fill.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: A structural, widening supply-demand gap in non-Russian enriched uranium is the core investment thesis for new enrichment entrants; watch fuel price spreads and Western enrichment capacity announcements as leading indicators.
insights.quote: The gap is just becoming bigger and bigger, and this technology is right in the middle.
insights.locator: Demand for fuel is increasing as countries look beyond Russia for uranium supply

themes.theme: Company Strategies: GLE vs. LIS Technologies

insights.claim: LIS Technologies, founded in 2023, purchased a 200-acre site in Oak Ridge, Tennessee and is in the pre-application process with the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission; it plans to enrich natural-grade uranium to roughly 5% U-235 for conventional reactor fuel, with an eventual goal of producing more concentrated material for next-generation reactors.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: LIS is pursuing the conventional freshly-mined-uranium enrichment market directly, competing with centrifuge incumbents on new-build capacity rather than reprocessing waste.

insights.claim: GLE is differentiating itself by reprocessing old uranium enrichment waste from the closed Paducah, Kentucky facility rather than enriching freshly mined material, effectively treating stockpiled tailings as a low-cost domestic feedstock source.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Reprocessing legacy waste sidesteps new-mining costs and permitting risk, giving GLE a potentially cheaper and faster path to feedstock than mined-uranium competitors.
insights.quote: It’s kind of like a large aboveground uranium mine for us.
insights.locator: GLE is taking a different approach

insights.claim: GLE holds a contract with the US Department of Energy to reprocess waste material at the Paducah enrichment site, where the facility could eventually process up to 200,000 metric tons of leftover material containing at least 0.25% U-235, enriching it to about 0.7%.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: A government contract and a large, already-mined feedstock base (200,000 metric tons) de-risk GLE's early-stage supply chain relative to greenfield mining-dependent competitors.
insights.locator: The company has a contract with the US Department of Energy

insights.claim: GLE completed a demonstration pilot in fall 2025 at its Wilmington, North Carolina testing facility, processing several hundred kilograms of uranium, then decommissioned that system and is building a new demonstration meant to show the technology works at commercial scale.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: The fall 2025 pilot is a concrete, checkable milestone; the next demonstration at commercial scale is the key near-term proof point to track before believing cost claims.
insights.locator: GLE has a testing facility in Wilmington, North Carolina

insights.claim: GLE CEO Stephen Long says the NRC's final safety evaluation for the Paducah facility should be finished in November 2026, final regulatory approval is expected in 2027, and the company plans to start processing material at the plant by 2030.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: This is a concrete regulatory and commercialization timeline (Nov 2026 safety evaluation, 2027 approval, 2030 start of processing) investors can use as milestones to track GLE's execution risk.
insights.locator: The final safety evaluation should be finished in November

insights.claim: Nuclear power currently supplies about 9% of global electricity, and that share could increase as major powers including the US and China build new reactors, including some based on next-generation technology.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: A rising nuclear share of global electricity generation underpins growing structural demand for enriched fuel, supporting the case for new enrichment capacity.
insights.locator: Nuclear power provides about 9% of global electricity today

insights.claim: Conventional reactors typically use low-enriched uranium around 5% U-235, but some advanced next-generation reactor designs require fuel enriched up to 20% U-235, meaning the shift toward advanced reactors will require higher-enrichment capacity than today's fleet.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Growth in advanced/next-gen reactor deployment implies rising demand specifically for higher-enrichment fuel, a segment new laser-enrichment entrants are explicitly targeting.
insights.locator: Today’s conventional reactors usually use low-enriched uranium

insights.claim: There is enough uranium on the planet to keep reactors running for decades, but as nuclear interest grows and enrichment geopolitics shift away from Russia, there could be short-term supply gaps or price spikes that alternative enrichment sources could help smooth out.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: The risk isn't a long-run uranium shortage but near-term enrichment bottlenecks and price volatility during the transition away from Russian supply — a window new enrichment capacity is racing to fill.
insights.locator: In the long run, there’s plenty of uranium on the planet

insights.claim: Laser enrichment plants could turn out to be cheaper than existing centrifuge technology, according to a senior fellow at the Nuclear Innovation Alliance, but the technology remains commercially unproven since it hasn't yet been built and operated at full scale.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Cost-advantage claims for laser enrichment remain unproven at scale; treat vendor and even independent-analyst cost projections as exploratory until a commercial plant is operating.
insights.quote: You don’t really know until you try to build one.
insights.locator: Laser enrichment plants could turn out to be cheaper than existing technologies
